questions.question: How do you write JSON responses in Go?
questions.title: Writing Json Responses
questions.direct_answer: Set the Content-Type header, then json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(v) — it marshals AND writes to the ResponseWriter in one step. Set the status first if non-200 (w.WriteHeader(200) before Encode).

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Set the Content-Type header, then json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(v) — it marshals AND writes to the ResponseWriter in one step. Set the status first if non-200 (w.WriteHeader(200) before Encode).

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The pattern, executed:

```go
func usersHandler(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(map[string]string{
        "name": "Al",
        "role": "dev",
    })
}
// GET /users → {"name":"Al","role":"dev"} with Content-Type: application/json — verified
```

The two steps in order: header, then encode. The header MUST be set before Encode writes (the body send flushes the headers — setting Content-Type after is a no-op).

With a status code (non-200):

```go
w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
w.WriteHeader(http.StatusCreated)  // 201
json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(user)
```

The order matters: Header() → WriteHeader() → Encode(). Once WriteHeader or the first write happens, headers are committed.

The error-response convention every API needs:

```go
func writeError(w http.ResponseWriter, status int, msg string) {
    w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    w.WriteHeader(status)
    json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(map[string]string{"error": msg})
}
```

The alternative: json.Marshal → w.Write(b) — the marshal-to-then-write form. Encoder is preferred (single step, streaming — writes as it marshals, no intermediate []byte allocation). The only reason to Marshal first: modifying the bytes (encryption, custom wrapping) or testing the marshal error separately.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    W[ResponseWriter] --> H[Header Set Content-Type]
    H --> S[WriteHeader 200]
    S --> E[json.NewEncoder w Encode v]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The Encoder's mechanics: json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(v) marshals v incrementally and writes directly to w — no intermediate buffer for the full JSON. The trade-off: you can't know the byte count ahead (no Content-Length from the encoder) — Go handles this with chunked transfer encoding for HTTP/1.1 (or streams for HTTP/2). For small responses, the difference is negligible; for large ones, the streaming avoids a full-copy.

The Encode error path, which people miss: Encode returns an error — but AFTER potentially writing partial bytes to w. The common handler ignores it (w is already committed — what would you do?). The honest pattern: for the critical first-write, Marshal first, check the error, then Write — for streaming large payloads, accept the partial-write-on-error semantics.

The API-envelope convention, worth naming as the architectural choice: many teams wrap all responses in {"data": ..., "error": ...} or the JSON:API format. The writeJSON helper encapsulates the decision:

```go
func writeJSON(w http.ResponseWriter, status int, v any) {
    w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    w.WriteHeader(status)
    json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(v)
}
```

One function, consistent ordering, every handler uses it — the bug (header after write) becomes structurally impossible.
